_notes: The 80 Pacific USA plants (ARCHITECTURE.md 11.3), in dex order by growth form:
1-40   trees
41-58  shrubs
59-77  herbs
78-80  ferns
plantClass is one of tree / shrub / herb / fern and is editorial judgment (growth
form, not taxonomy — DESIGN.md D13). Ecosystem tags are judgment too, never fetched.
'edible' is the curator's ONLY use tag. The 'medicinal' tag is derived at build time
from Dr. Duke's ethnobotanical records and is not an input field; a genuine
disagreement is pinned with overrides.medicinal.
'usesNote' is required when edible is true (name the part and the season) and
whenever Duke's records the species as a poison (then it must contain a sentence
beginning 'Caution:'). It is <= 240 characters, and is forbidden when the species
ends up with no use tag at all.
'dukeName' pins the Duke's join for a species Duke's files under an older name.
'wikipediaTitle' pins the article; 'overrides' pins any output field.
SAFETY: these notes are the only unsourced text in the catalogue. They name a part
and a season and nothing more, they never say a plant is safe, and every species
with a toxic part or a dangerous lookalike carries a 'Caution:' sentence whether or
not Duke's flags it. See DESIGN.md D14/M30 and ARCHITECTURE.md R11.

species.usesNote: Caution: the needles are recorded as poisonous and are a known cause of abortion in grazing cattle. Nothing from this tree is a food, and the traditional uses below are records, not recommendations.
Pine nuts from the cones, early autumn — the ripe cones are heated or dried until they open, and the shelled seeds are eaten raw or roasted.
Caution: the foliage is rich in thujone and is toxic taken internally; the wood dust irritates skin and airways. This tree is not a food.

Bright new needle tips, spring — a few picked young for tea or syrup. Caution: yew looks similar to an untrained eye and is deadly; take tips only from a tree whose needles are stiff, sharp and four-sided.

Caution: every part of this tree is deadly poisonous — needles, bark, wood, and the seed inside the red berry-like aril. Nothing from it is a food, and the recorded uses below are history, not a recommendation.
Caution: recorded as poisonous. The foliage and cones are not a food, and the sawdust and foliage oil irritate skin and airways.
Acorns, autumn — shelled, ground and leached in many changes of water until no bitterness is left, then cooked. Caution: raw acorns are heavy with tannin and are not eaten.
Acorns, autumn — the sweetest of the local oaks, but still shelled, ground and leached in many changes of water before cooking. Caution: raw acorns are not eaten.
Acorns, autumn — shelled, ground and leached in many changes of water until no bitterness is left, then cooked. Caution: raw acorns are heavy with tannin and are not eaten.
Small red berries, autumn — dry and mealy raw, and usually dried or cooked before eating.
Sap, late winter — tapped and boiled down to syrup; the hanging flower clusters are also eaten cooked in early spring.

overrides.habitatText: Streambanks, sloughs, wet meadows and lake margins from Alaska south through the Pacific states and east to the Rockies, at low to middle elevations.

species._comment: GBIF lumps this into Salix lucida, and the Wikipedia article covers that whole complex — 'shining willow, Pacific willow, red willow'. The entry therefore ships GBIF's accepted species name rather than the subspecies trinomial, so the name and the source article agree. No article for subsp. lasiandra exists to pin. The habitat text is written rather than fetched because the article's is about the complex.

species.usesNote: Leaves, any season — far stronger than kitchen bay; one small leaf does the work of several. Caution: the fresh crushed leaves give some people a severe headache, and the raw leaf is too strong to eat whole.
Small tart apples, late summer into autumn — eaten once softened on the tree or by frost, or cooked; the seeds are discarded as with any apple.

overrides.habitatText: Streamsides, canyon bottoms and floodplains through the coast ranges, the Central Valley and the Sierra foothills of California and into northern Baja California, wherever its roots can reach year-round groundwater. Widely planted in the same range as a street and park tree.

species.usesNote: Dark blue-black berries, late summer — eaten fresh, dried into cakes or cooked down into jam.
Small black berries, late summer into autumn — sweetest after the first frosts; eaten fresh or cooked.
Translucent red berries, summer — sharply tart, eaten fresh or cooked into jelly.
Amber to red raspberry-like fruit, late spring into early summer — eaten fresh; the peeled young shoots are also eaten in spring.
Soft red fruit, mid to late summer — eaten fresh off the plant; it is far too fragile to carry home.

overrides.habitatText: Roadsides, fence lines, riverbanks, forest edges and waste ground throughout the lowland Pacific states, where it forms dense impenetrable thickets. Introduced from the Caucasus and thoroughly naturalised west of the Cascades.

species.usesNote: Blackberries, late summer into autumn — eaten fresh or cooked. Introduced and invasive here, so picking it does the thicket no harm.
Berries, late summer to early autumn — cooked or dried before eating; flowers for cordial and tea. Caution: raw berries, leaves, stems and bark are toxic, and red-berried elders are not this species.

Blue-purple berries, late summer — very tart and full of seeds, so they are cooked with sugar into jelly rather than eaten raw. Caution: the yellow root and bark are bitter with berberine and are not a food.

overrides.habitatText: Chaparral and dry foothill woodland on rocky, well-drained slopes, through the inner North Coast Ranges of California and the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, mostly below about 1,200 metres.

species.usesNote: Berries, late summer — dry and mealy; traditionally crushed and steeped in cold water for a cider-like drink rather than eaten whole.
Red berries, late autumn into winter — always cooked or dried first. Caution: the raw fruit and the leaves hold cyanide-releasing compounds and are not eaten raw.
Purple berries, midsummer — sweet and mild, eaten fresh, dried or cooked.
Hips, autumn into winter — the outer flesh is eaten or steeped for tea, and the petals in early summer. Caution: the seeds and their irritant hairs inside the hip are scraped out and discarded.
Blue-black berries under a white bloom, midsummer — edible but dry and insipid, and usually cooked rather than eaten fresh.
Dark red to black cherries, late summer — cooked and strained for jelly or syrup. Caution: the pits, leaves and twigs hold cyanide-releasing compounds and are never crushed or eaten.
Caution: fresh cascara bark is a violent purgative and was traditionally aged a year or more before any use at all. Nothing from this shrub is a food.
Caution: recorded as poisonous, and every stem and leaf is armoured with brittle spines that break off in the skin. The traditional uses below are a record of practice, not a recommendation.
The whole leafy rosette, late winter into spring — eaten raw as salad or briefly cooked; it turns bitter once the plant flowers and the weather warms.
Young leaves and tops, early spring before flowering — cooking or drying destroys the sting. Caution: the fresh plant stings on contact, and older flowering plants are not eaten.

Bulbs, dug after the flowers fade in summer — slow-baked for many hours; raw they are indigestible. Caution: deadly death camas shares these meadows, so dig only bulbs marked while the blue flowers were open.
Young shoots, spring — cooked like asparagus before the leaves open; the leaves and flowers are dried for tea later in the summer.
Caution: wild gingers contain aristolochic acid, which damages the kidneys and causes cancer. Despite a long history as a flavouring and a remedy, this plant is not eaten. It is not culinary ginger.
Small red berries, summer — eaten fresh; far smaller and more strongly flavoured than a garden strawberry.

Young shoot hearts in spring and green flower spikes in early summer — peeled and cooked. Caution: before the brown spike shows, cattail is easily confused with iris, whose leaves and rhizomes are poisonous.

Starchy tubers, autumn into early spring — dug from the mud and always cooked, never raw. Caution: gather only where you saw the arrowhead leaves and three white petals, and never from polluted water.
Leaves, any season — a trailing woodland mint, steeped fresh or dried for tea rather than eaten as a food.
Caution: this poppy carries sedative alkaloids and Duke's itself lists it as cyanogenetic. It is not a food, and it is the California state flower — leave it where it grows.

Bulbs and leaves, spring into summer — used like a mild onion. Caution: deadly death camas grows alongside and looks similar out of flower; if the crushed plant does not smell of onion, it is not this plant.
Leafy stems, autumn through spring — eaten raw or lightly cooked. Caution: poisonous scarlet pimpernel grows in the same ground; chickweed has one line of fine hairs running up one side of the stem.
Leaves in early spring before the plant blooms, the flower heads in spring, the root roasted in autumn. Caution: not picked from lawns or verges that may have been sprayed.

overrides.habitatText: Cool, clear, slow-moving fresh water — spring heads, creek margins, seeps and ditches — where it roots in gravel and forms floating mats. Native to Eurasia and thoroughly naturalised across the Pacific states.

species.usesNote: Leafy stems, the cool months — cooked rather than raw when wild. Caution: deadly water hemlock grows in the same streams, and cress from water below livestock can carry liver fluke.
Rhizome, autumn through spring — a small piece chewed for its sweet liquorice taste and spat out; it is a flavouring, not a food.
Caution: bracken fiddleheads are eaten in several cuisines, but the plant contains ptaquiloside, an established carcinogen that cooking only reduces. This catalogue does not tag it edible.
